title: Born in Bethlehem, Presented in the Temple
summary: A census decreed by Caesar Augustus brings Joseph and the pregnant Mary to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger. Angels announce the birth to shepherds, who come and find the child. Forty days later his parents present him in the temple, where the aged Simeon and the prophetess Anna recognize him as God's salvation. At twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple after Passover, and when his anxious parents find him among the teachers, he says he had to be in his Father's house.
story: Chapter 1 announced two births; chapter 2 tells the greater one. Luke sets the birth of Jesus against the background of the Roman Empire, so that the emperor's decree moves a village couple to David's town, fulfilling a promise Augustus never heard of. The chapter then returns to the temple, where Luke's story began, and to faithful Israelites who were waiting for God's consolation. Simeon's words widen the horizon: this child is a light for the Gentiles as well as the glory of Israel, and he will cause the rise and fall of many. The chapter closes with the only story in the Gospels from Jesus' childhood, which shows him already aware of his unique relation to his Father, and then with eighteen silent years in Nazareth before John appears in chapter 3.
historical:
Caesar Augustus, born Octavian, the adopted heir of Julius Caesar, ruled the Roman world from 31 BC to AD 14. His reign was celebrated as an age of peace, and inscriptions honored him as a savior who had brought good news; one from Priene in Asia Minor, dated to 9 BC, calls his birthday the beginning of good news for the world. Luke's angel announces a different Savior and different good news. Augustus did order censuses: he records three counts of Roman citizens, and provincial censuses for taxation were carried out in various regions during his reign. Papyri from Roman Egypt show that households there were required to register every fourteen years, and a governor's edict from AD 104 orders people to return to their homes for a census.

The mention of Quirinius raises a known historical difficulty. Publius Sulpicius Quirinius became governor (legate) of Syria in AD 6, and Josephus describes a census he conducted in Judea that year, when Rome began ruling Judea directly after deposing Herod's son Archelaus. But Luke 1:5 and Matthew 2 place Jesus' birth in the reign of Herod the Great, who died in 4 BC. The main solutions are set out in the hard question below.
cultural:
Joseph went to Bethlehem, a small town about six miles south of Jerusalem, because it was David's hometown and his family's place of origin. The word traditionally translated inn (kataluma) is the same word Luke uses for the upper guest room of the Last Supper (22:11). Many interpreters therefore think Joseph and Mary stayed with relatives whose guest room was full, and that the child was laid in a feeding trough in the family area of the house, where animals were often brought in at night in village homes, rather than in a stable behind a commercial inn. Swaddling cloths were strips of cloth wrapped snugly around a newborn, a normal act of care. Shepherds worked long hours outdoors, and while David was a shepherd, the occupation carried little status; later rabbinic sources are suspicious of herdsmen. The text gives no date for the birth, and the December date was set by the church centuries later.

The Law of Moses required a mother to wait forty days after the birth of a son before offering a sacrifice for her purification (Leviticus 12), and allowed the poor to bring two birds instead of a lamb (Leviticus 12:8), which tells us about Joseph and Mary's means. Every firstborn son belonged to God and was redeemed by a payment (Exodus 13:2, Numbers 18:15-16). Faithful Jews went up to Jerusalem for Passover each year, and pilgrims from Galilee traveled together in large groups of family and neighbors, which explains how a twelve-year-old could be missed for a day.
literary: The chapter is framed by the emperor's decree and the temple. Its three scenes (the birth, the presentation, the boy in the temple) each end with a response: the shepherds glorify God, Simeon and Anna give thanks, and the teachers are astounded. Mary appears twice treasuring these things in her heart (verses 19 and 51), a hint that she was among Luke's sources. Luke pairs Simeon and Anna, a man and a woman, as he often does. Simeon's song (verses 29 to 32), called the Nunc Dimittis from its first words in Latin, draws on Isaiah, where God's servant is made a light for the nations (Isaiah 42:6, 49:6). The chapter's last verse echoes the description of the boy Samuel in 1 Samuel 2:26, who grew in stature and in favor with the Lord and with man. The first words Luke gives from Jesus himself are in verse 49, and they concern his Father.

outline.t: The census and the birth in Bethlehem
The boy Jesus in the temple

doctrines.note: The angel announces a Savior who is Christ the Lord, born for all the people, and Simeon holds the child and says, my eyes have seen your salvation. Salvation in Luke is not first an idea but a person, and it arrives as good news of great joy.

Simeon calls Jesus a light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory to Israel. From the first week of his life the salvation he brings is meant for the nations, which Luke's second volume, Acts, will show coming true.

Jesus' parents do everything the Law of the Lord requires: circumcision on the eighth day, purification, presentation of the firstborn, and the yearly Passover. Luke shows the Savior born under the law and raised in faithful obedience to it, within Israel's worship.

He is born in the city of David and called Christ the Lord, joining the royal title with the divine name. Simeon had been promised he would see the Lord's Christ, and at twelve Jesus speaks of God as his own Father.

words.note: Soter, savior or deliverer. The Greek Old Testament uses it of God, and the Roman world used it of rulers and gods, including Augustus. In the Gospels it appears only in Luke's first two chapters and once in John. The angel's announcement quietly contrasts two claims: the emperor in Rome, and the child in a manger.

Kataluma, a lodging place or guest room. It is the word for the room where Jesus eats the Last Supper (22:11), while Luke uses a different word for the inn in the parable of the Good Samaritan (10:34). This supports the reading that there was no room in the family guest room, not that a commercial innkeeper turned them away.

Eudokia, good pleasure or favor. The angels' song blesses peace on earth to people of God's favor. Later manuscripts read a slightly different form that gives the familiar goodwill toward men, but the earliest texts point to people on whom God's favor rests. The peace is God's gift to those he has chosen, not a general mood.

Dei, it is necessary, I must. Jesus' first recorded words use it: I had to be in my Father's house. The same word will mark his sense of divine purpose throughout Luke, from preaching the kingdom (4:43) to his suffering and rising (9:22, 24:7, 24:26). Even as a boy he knows he is under his Father's necessity.

christ: Luke 2 shows the Son of God entering the world in poverty and obscurity. He is laid in a feeding trough, visited by shepherds, and redeemed with a poor family's offering, yet angels proclaim him Savior, Christ, and Lord. He fulfills the promise that the ruler of Israel would come from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), and in Simeon's words he is the servant of Isaiah 49:6, a light for the nations. Simeon also speaks of opposition and a sword that will pierce Mary's soul, the first shadow of the cross in Luke. At twelve Jesus calls God my Father and grows in wisdom and favor, fully human in his development, and yet already the Son who belongs in his Father's house. The church confesses both truths together: he is truly God and truly man, who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7).

hard.q: How can Luke date Jesus' birth to a census under Quirinius when Quirinius governed Syria in AD 6, about ten years after Herod the Great died?
hard.a: The difficulty is real, and scholars answer it in several ways. First, many critical scholars conclude that Luke made a mistake, confusing the well-known census of AD 6, which provoked the revolt of Judas the Galilean, with the time of Jesus' birth; they add that a Roman census in Herod's kingdom, which was a client kingdom rather than a province, would have been unusual. Second, some argue that verse 2 can be translated differently: the Greek word usually rendered first can also mean before, giving this census took place before Quirinius was governor of Syria, distinguishing it from the famous later one. Grammarians debate whether that reading is natural. Third, some propose that Quirinius held an earlier command or official role in the region in the last years BC, since he was active in the East in that period, and that Luke uses the word governor loosely for that office. The evidence for such an earlier post is disputed. Fourth, some suggest that a registration begun under Herod was completed, or became known, under Quirinius. The church father Tertullian, around AD 200, linked the census with Sentius Saturninus, who governed Syria about 9 to 6 BC, which may reflect a separate tradition. Luke elsewhere shows careful knowledge of Roman officials and titles, which gives some readers reason to give him the benefit of the doubt, while others think the tension cannot be resolved with the evidence now available. The question concerns a date; it does not affect the gospel's confession that Jesus was born in David's town as a real man in real history.

questions: The birth of the Savior was announced first to shepherds, not to rulers or priests. What does that suggest about who God's good news is for, and whether you would have heard it?
Simeon and Anna waited for years in prayer and worship before they saw what they hoped for. What helps you keep hoping when God's promises seem slow?
Mary treasured and pondered what she did not yet understand. What experiences of God in your life are you still pondering?
